extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, advanced mathematics students, and applied statisticians (readers of the American Mathematical Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Reflections on practices for developing mathematical theorems: ordering problem/theorem/proof/definitions, using counterexamples to refine statements, and the role of computational/empirical experimentation in mathematical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of mathematical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: First the problem, then the theorem, then the proof, with the definition at the very end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gelman argues that definitions should come at the end because they represent the minimal conditions under which the theorem is true; the conventional order (definitions, lemmas, theorems, proofs) hides this development. Present the problem before stating the theorem so the theorem and its scope can be shaped by attempts at proof and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions as minimal conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions come at the end because they represent the minimal conditions under which the theorem is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat definitions as outcomes of the proof/counterexample process: they should capture the minimal assumptions needed. As theory expands, definitions become more specific. Definitions are dual to counterexamples: counterexamples expose which aspects must be included in the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem statement should evolve
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of the theorem itself changes as the proof and definitions develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to revise the theorem in response to attempted proofs and discovered counterexamples rather than fixing a final statement at the outset. The evolving statement reflects discovery of the precise conditions under which the result holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to bound scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem is bounded by its counterexamples, which are duals to its definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek counterexamples to delineate the limits of a conjecture; each counterexample helps define what must be excluded or added to hypotheses. The practice of identifying counterexamples is central to refining both theorems and definitions (illustrated by the many counterexamples to Euler's polyhedron formula).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs-and-refutations as methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop results through an iterative process of proposing proofs, encountering counterexamples, and rescuing or reformulating the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos's dialogic method (as recounted) brings up counterexamples, attempts to rescue the theorem, and refines concepts; this empirical, iterative approach is a legitimate and productive style of mathematical practice. Use historical and hypothetical dialogues to explore how concepts and proofs can evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against ad-hoc exception-barring and monster-barring
rubrics_metrics.description: Exception-barring and monster-barring are strategies used to rescue the theorem from counterexamples but incur increasing costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the anti-pattern of salvaging a theorem via ad-hoc exceptions that complicate or undermine its explanatory power. Prefer principled refinement of definitions and hypotheses over repeatedly carving out special cases unless those cases indicate a genuine structural distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of definitions should be pragmatic and scalable
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical definitions are as precise as they need to be; as the theory is expanded, definitions become more specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the level of precision appropriate to the current stage of theory development. Expect and allow for increasing specificity: early formulations may be looser and later tightened in response to counterexamples and further theory-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate empirical/computational experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The effectiveness of scientific inquiry (including computer experimentation) is relevant in mathematical research and in developing statistical methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use computational experiments and empirical checks as part of the discovery process—especially in modern practice—to generate conjectures, find counterexamples, and test proposed methods. For applied statisticians, alternate cycles of proposing methods and confronting them with real problems mirror proofs-and-refutations.
